screens.title: Leveraging the sys Schema for Simplified Analysis
screens.narratorSegment: The sys schema is an essential convenience layer built on top of Performance Schema that makes raw instrumentation useful without heavy S Q L. In this lesson you will learn why sys exists, what it does for DBAs, and the practical views you will reach for during day-to-day troubleshooting. Think of sys as a translator: it aggregates events, formats latency and memory metrics, and exposes user-friendly views so you can focus on analysis rather than joins. For example, instead of writing several joins across events_statements_history and threads, you can query sys. statements_with_runtimes_in_host to surface the statements ranked by average latency. That reduces both time and error when hunting slow queries or tracking input and output hot spots. We will also cover how to check active sessions with sys. processlist, how to read file-level input and output with io_global_by_file_by_latency, and how to interpret memory allocations via memory_global_by_current_bytes. Finally, you will learn common pitfalls: sys does not collect extra data and depends entirely on Performance Schema instrumentation, and sometimes you must dive into the raw tables for the deepest analysis. By the end of the lesson you will know when sys is sufficient and when to step down into raw Performance Schema data.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: sys schema simplifies Performance Schema by aggregating and formatting instrumented data into readable views, speeding common DBA analysis.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › Leveraging the sys Schema
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Turn instrumented data into answers

This chapter shows how sys schema presents aggregated, human-readable views built on Performance Schema so you can quickly locate slow statements, costly I/O, and memory hotspots.

In this lesson
  • Understand sys as an abstraction layer over Performance Schema.
  • Use key views: processlist, statements, I/O, and memory summaries.
  • Configure sys variables and avoid common misconfigurations.
Why this matters

Faster diagnostics mean less downtime and quicker tuning decisions. sys reduces query complexity and highlights the metrics DBAs need first.

Visual: sys as translator

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: Over these screens you will develop practical skills for monitoring and troubleshooting with the sys schema. First, you will be able to explain the purpose and benefits of sys and how it relies on Performance Schema instrumentation. You will practice identifying the most useful sys views for monitoring active sessions, input and output, and memory. You will also learn how to find slow statements quickly using runtime views and full-table-scan reports. Finally, you will see which configurable sys variables affect reporting and history size and how to change them safely. Each objective ties directly to routine DBA tasks: checking active client activity during outage, finding queries for index tuning, pinpointing a noisy file causing input and output latency, and adjusting instrumentation history to retain useful details. Along the way you'll learn to spot a common misconception: sys does not capture additional events—it only presents what Performance Schema already gathers. Understanding that boundary helps you decide when sys alone is enough and when to inspect raw Performance Schema tables for deeper troubleshooting.

screens.title: What is the sys schema?
screens.narratorSegment: The sys schema is a curated set of views, functions, and procedures that present Performance Schema data in an aggregated, readable format. In short, it does not collect new events; it reshapes and summarizes the data Performance Schema already captures. A useful analogy is to think of Performance Schema as an instrumented raw log and sys as a set of report templates that turn that log into charts and tables you can read quickly. This means sys saves you time when you need high-level answers — like which queries are slow or which files have the most input and output latency — because the heavy lifting of joins and unit conversions is already done for you. For example, instead of computing average latencies from multiple events tables, you can query statements_with_runtimes_in_host and see avg_latency and max_latency ready to act on. A common misconception is that sys reduces the need to learn Performance Schema; it does not. If you need the lowest-level detail — for instance the exact events or raw wait instances — you must query the Performance Schema tables directly. The practical takeaway is to use sys for routine diagnosis and only step down into raw tables when a deeper, granular trace is required. Try to internalize that boundary now: sys simplifies analysis, Performance Schema provides depth.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › What is the sys schema?
Formal definition

A collection of views, functions, and procedures built on Performance Schema to present aggregated, human-readable performance metrics.

Analogy

Performance Schema is raw instrumentation; sys provides report templates that summarize and format that instrumentation for quick answers.

When to use sys
  • Daily checks for slow queries and active sessions.
  • Quick I/O and memory hotspot identification.
  • Initial triage before deeper Performance Schema analysis.
Example
-- Find top statements by average latency
SELECT
  query,
  db,
  full_scan,
  exec_count,
  total_latency,
  avg_latency,
  max_latency
FROM
  sys.statements_with_runtimes_in_host
ORDER BY
  avg_latency DESC
LIMIT 10;
This view already exposes avg_latency and exec_count so you can rank problem statements without manual joins.
Misconception

Do not assume sys creates additional instrumentation. If Performance Schema instruments are disabled, sys views return empty or incomplete results.

Key Takeaway

Use sys for fast, high-level diagnostics. Drop into Performance Schema for the most granular investigation.

screens.title: Inspecting active sessions with sys.processlist
screens.narratorSegment: When you need to quickly see what the server is doing, sys. processlist is a more usable view than SHOW PROCESSLIST because it provides richer columns and is easier to filter. The typical workflow is to run a SELECT that omits sleeping connections, sort by running time, and inspect the current_statement, state, and time columns. For example, a common triage query selects thd_id, conn_id, user, db, command, state, time, and current_statement and orders by time descending to reveal long-running work. Use this output to spot blocked or stuck queries and note the program or user responsible. A concrete example: after executing a few simple selects and a deliberate sleep, run the provided query and observe a row where command is not Sleep and time is several seconds — that identifies the simulated long-running query. A misconception to watch is assuming high time always means heavy resource use; sometimes a thread waits for a lock with low C P U but high wait time. The key skill is correlating state, current_statement, and time to determine whether to kill, tune, or investigate further. Practice by running the example and describing the state and likely next action for any long entry you find.

keyIdea.title: Practical query
keyIdea.text: Use sys.processlist to surface non-sleeping threads ordered by running time to identify long-running or blocked connections.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › sys.processlist walkthrough
Query to run
SELECT
    thd_id,
    conn_id,
    user,
    db,
    command,
    state,
    time,
    current_statement,
    program
FROM
    sys.processlist
WHERE
    command != 'Sleep'
ORDER BY
    time DESC
LIMIT 10;
How to interpret
  • time shows how long the thread has been in its current state.
  • state explains the wait or active phase, e.g., Waiting for table metadata lock.
  • current_statement reveals the SQL you might tune or kill.
Common pitfall

High time does not always indicate CPU usage; it can be a lock wait. Cross-check state and other metrics before terminating connections.

Sample output (simulated)
thd_id | conn_id | user | db | command | state | time | current_statement ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ 1001 | 55 | app | orders| Query | Sending data | 12 | SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id=42 1002 | 56 | app | NULL | Query | Waiting for table metadata lock | 8 | ALTER TABLE shipments ADD COLUMN
From this output, the first row shows a running SELECT taking 12 seconds; the second indicates a metadata lock wait which likely blocks DDL.
Takeaway

Use processlist to prioritize actions: tune long-running queries, investigate lock waits, or identify misbehaving programs.

screens.title: Finding slow statements with runtime views
screens.narratorSegment: To prioritize tuning, start by ranking statements by average latency. The sys. statements_with_runtimes_in_host view exposes avg_latency, total_latency, exec_count, and max_latency so you can see both typical and worst-case behavior. A practical query selects query, db, full_scan, exec_count, total_latency, avg_latency, and max_latency and orders by avg_latency descending. When you run that, look for statements with both high avg_latency and significant exec_count; those are excellent optimization candidates because they compound cost. A concrete scenario: if a reporting query runs often during peak traffic and shows high avg_latency, consider adding indexes, rewriting joins, or breaking the report into smaller queries. A common misconception is to optimize queries with a single high max_latency but zero exec_count; always consider frequency. Also check the full_scan flag — statements that frequently perform full table scans are top candidates for index intervention. Finally, remember that sys aggregates by text; when many similar parameterized statements appear as one row, consider looking at the raw Performance Schema for per-thread detail. The core skill is ranking by avg_latency, correlating with exec_count and full_scan, and creating an actionable list for tuning. Finding slow statements with runtime views means rank by avg_latency and factor in exec_count and full_scan to prioritize which queries to tune first.. In practical terms, use statements_with_runtimes_in_host to rank expensive queries. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Ranking queries
keyIdea.text: Rank by avg_latency and factor in exec_count and full_scan to prioritize which queries to tune first.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › Finding slow statements
Query to rank by avg latency
SELECT
    query,
    db,
    full_scan,
    exec_count,
    total_latency,
    avg_latency,
    max_latency
FROM
    sys.statements_with_runtimes_in_host
ORDER BY
    avg_latency DESC
LIMIT 10;
Interpretation tips
  • High avg_latency + high exec_count = prime tuning target.
  • full_scan true indicates likely indexing issues.
  • Use max_latency to find outliers and avg_latency for typical cost.
Misconception

Don't optimize solely for the single highest max_latency; frequency matters. A rare spike can mislead prioritization.

Example analysis
Suppose a query shows avg_latency 500ms and exec_count 2000. That represents sustained cost. A different query with max_latency 5000ms but exec_count 2 may be less urgent.
-- Action list 1. Run EXPLAIN for top queries 2. Check indexes or rewrite joins 3. Re-test and monitor avg_latency
Key Takeaway

Combine avg_latency with exec_count and full_scan to create a prioritized tuning backlog you can act on immediately.

screens.title: Finding full-table scans and errors
screens.narratorSegment: Some sys views focus on specific problems. For example, sys. statements_with_full_table_scans collects statements that performed full table scans, exposing full_scan_count, exec_count, and latencies. Another useful view is sys. statements_with_errors_or_warnings, which surfaces statements that caused errors or warnings. The comparison approach is to use the focused view when you have a hypothesis. If slow reports point to scanning behavior, query the full_table_scans view and order by full_scan_count to find the most frequent offenders. If an application reports errors, check the errors_or_warnings view to find statements that generate those events and correlate with user reports. A concrete example: ordering by full_scan_count descending will show a frequently scanned query that might benefit from an index. A misconception is to treat these focused views as exhaustive—they summarize events that Performance Schema recorded, so missing instrumentation or disabled instruments will hide problems. When you need row-level or event-level detail, drill into the underlying Performance Schema tables. Use these focused sys views as targeted shortcuts: they narrow the search space and give actionable columns such as full_scan_count and exec_count for prioritization. Finding full-table scans and errors means use statements_with_full_table_scans and statements_with_errors_or_warnings to quickly find frequent full scans or problem-generating statements.. In practical terms, use dedicated sys views to surface problematic statements. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Targeted views
keyIdea.text: Use statements_with_full_table_scans and statements_with_errors_or_warnings to quickly find frequent full scans or problem-generating statements.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › Full-table scans & errors
Full-table scan query
SELECT
  query,
  db,
  exec_count,
  full_scan_count,
  total_latency,
  avg_latency
FROM
  sys.statements_with_full_table_scans
ORDER BY
  full_scan_count DESC
LIMIT 5;
When to use

Run this when you suspect missing indexes or queries scanning large tables frequently, especially during load spikes.

Errors or warnings query
SELECT
  query,
  db,
  count_star AS occurrences,
  last_error
FROM
  sys.statements_with_errors_or_warnings
ORDER BY
  occurrences DESC
LIMIT 10;
Misconception

These views show what was recorded. If Performance Schema filters or instruments are off, statements may be missing from these summaries.

Example action

For a query with high full_scan_count, run EXPLAIN, add indexes, or rewrite the query, then re-check the sys view for improvement.

screens.title: Analyzing I/O by file
screens.narratorSegment: Disk activity often explains slow queries more than S Q L structure alone. The sys. io_global_by_file_by_latency view aggregates input and output per file and provides total_read_bytes, total_written_bytes, and total_latency so you can see which files cause the most latency. A typical analysis selects file, total_read_bytes divided to megabytes, total_written_bytes to megabytes, and total_latency converted to milliseconds, ordering by total_latency descending to highlight the most latency-prone files. For instance, InnoDB data files or binary logs may show as top latency contributors. Once you identify a hot file, correlate it with MySQL configuration, file placement, or underlying storage health. It could indicate a need to move data files to faster storage, tune checkpointing settings, or investigate OS-level contention. A common mistake is to interpret high bytes transferred as the same as high latency; high throughput is normal for busy databases, but high total_latency points to delays. Use both bytes and latency together: high latency with modest bytes often means seeks or IO wait; high bytes with low latency suggests healthy throughput. The practical outcome is a prioritized list of files to investigate with storage and input and output tuning actions.

keyIdea.title: I/O metrics
keyIdea.text: Rank files by total_latency and consider read/write volume to decide whether latency originates from throughput or storage contention.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › I/O analysis
I/O query
SELECT
    file,
    total_read_bytes / 1024 / 1024 AS total_read_mb,
    total_written_bytes / 1024 / 1024 AS total_written_mb,
    total_latency / 1000000000 AS total_latency_ms
FROM
    sys.io_global_by_file_by_latency
ORDER BY
    total_latency DESC
LIMIT 10;
Interpretation
  • total_latency_ms shows aggregate waiting time for I/O on a file.
  • Compare latency with read/write MB to differentiate throughput vs wait issues.
  • Investigate high-latency files in storage and OS layers.
Example scenario
If an InnoDB data file shows total_latency_ms high but read_mb moderate, the storage may be suffering random IO waits. If binlog shows high written_mb with low latency, focus elsewhere.
-- Action checklist 1. Identify top files by latency 2. Check storage metrics and queue depth 3. Consider moving heavy files to faster media or tuning flushing 4. Re-evaluate latency after changes
Key Takeaway

Use both latency and bytes to diagnose whether storage or workload patterns cause observed slowness, then coordinate with ops for remediation.

screens.title: Inspecting memory consumption
screens.narratorSegment: Memory pressure can cause instability and degraded performance. The sys. memory_global_by_current_bytes view reports current_alloc_bytes and high_alloc_bytes so you can see current allocations and recorded high-water marks across components. A useful query selects event_name, current_alloc_bytes / 1024 / 1024 as current_alloc_mb, and high_alloc_bytes / 1024 / 1024 as high_alloc_mb, ordered by current_alloc_bytes descending to surface the biggest consumers. For example, internal buffers or caches may appear as top consumers and point to configuration areas to tune. When you see a component with a large difference between high_alloc and current_alloc, it suggests bursts of activity or temporary spikes; an always-high current_alloc indicates sustained consumption that might require configuration changes. A common misconception is assuming memory reported here directly equals OS process resident memory. These are allocations tracked by Performance Schema for internal components and threads; you still must correlate with OS-level tools for total process memory. The practical path is: identify large allocators in sys, review MySQL configuration or workload causing them, then test changes on a staging instance before production. This view helps make informed memory tuning decisions and avoid out-of-memory surprises.

keyIdea.title: Memory insight
keyIdea.text: Use current and high alloc metrics to distinguish sustained memory usage from spikes and guide tuning or capacity planning.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › Memory analysis
Memory query
SELECT
    event_name,
    current_alloc_bytes / 1024 / 1024 AS current_alloc_mb,
    high_alloc_bytes / 1024 / 1024 AS high_alloc_mb
FROM
    sys.memory_global_by_current_bytes
ORDER BY
    current_alloc_bytes DESC
LIMIT 10;
How to use
  • Spot the largest current allocators to guide tuning.
  • Compare high_alloc to current_alloc for burst behavior.
  • Correlate with workload patterns and configuration settings.
Example interpretation
A component with high_alloc_mb 1024 but current_alloc_mb 128 indicates occasional peaks. If current_alloc_mb stays high across sampling windows, that may justify raising memory limits or changing buffer sizes.
-- Practical steps 1. Run the memory query during normal and peak times 2. Identify components with sustained high current_alloc 3. Tune related configuration or reduce workload intensity 4. Re-run and verify reductions
Misconception

These allocations reflect tracked internal allocations in Performance Schema, not the entire process RSS. Always cross-check with OS tools for total memory usage.

screens.title: Configuring sys schema behavior
screens.narratorSegment: sys exposes a few variables you can set to control how its views behave, such as ps_setup_size_statements_history which controls how much statement history to keep, and ps_thread_account_for_background_threads which affects whether background threads are included in some aggregations. Use SET GLOBAL sys. variable_name = value to change these settings. The safe process is: first understand your workload and why you need more or less history, then change the variable in a non-production environment and observe effects on view contents and Performance Schema overhead. A concrete example: increasing ps_setup_size_statements_history retains more statements for sys views, which can help with post-facto investigation but increases memory and storage used by Performance Schema. A common pitfall is adjusting these variables without checking Performance Schema instrumentation — if the underlying instruments are not enabled, increasing history does not create data. Another pitfall is to raise history size on a very busy system without capacity planning, which can increase memory pressure. The practical guidance is to document any change, monitor memory and query instrumentation impact, and roll back if Performance Schema metrics show undue overhead. Use sys settings to make views more informative, but always balance visibility with resource cost.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › Configuring sys
Common variables
ps_setup_size_statements_history — controls how much statement history is retained
ps_thread_account_for_background_threads — include background threads in some aggregations
Change pattern
  1. Plan and document desired setting changes.
  2. Test in a staging environment with similar load.
  3. Monitor Performance Schema overhead and memory.
  4. Apply to production during a maintenance window if safe.
Example command
-- Increase statement history size SET GLOBAL sys.ps_setup_size_statements_history = 10000;
After this change, sys views that rely on statement history will have more retained entries. Monitor memory use closely.
Common mistake

Changing history size without enabling the required Performance Schema instruments yields no extra data but may consume memory when instruments are active.

screens.title: sys schema vs raw Performance Schema
screens.narratorSegment: Deciding between using sys and directly querying Performance Schema depends on the level of detail you need. Use sys when you want aggregated, human-friendly summaries for common tasks like ranking slow queries, seeing active sessions, or locating input and output and memory hotspots. The benefit is speed: queries are shorter and results are already formatted. However, sys does not replace Performance Schema for event-level analysis. When you need exact event timing, per-thread stack traces, or low-level wait instances, raw Performance Schema tables such as events_statements_history or events_waits_history provide the granularity sys abstracts away. A practical example: if sys shows a statement with high avg_latency but multiple parameterized variants are aggregated together, stepping down to events_statements_history will show per-thread or per-event details and reveal which parameter values trigger poor performance. A common misconception is that sys is always sufficient for any performance problem; it is not. The pattern to adopt is: start with sys for quick triage, then drill into Performance Schema when sys answers are insufficient. This two-level approach balances speed with depth and prevents wasted time writing complex joins for routine checks.

keyIdea.text: Start with sys for quick triage and use Performance Schema raw tables for event-level, granular troubleshooting when needed.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › sys vs Performance Schema
sys — what it gives you
  • Aggregated, formatted metrics ready for ranking.
  • Simpler queries for common DBA workflows.
  • Views tailored to sessions, statements, I/O, and memory.
Performance Schema — what it gives you
  • Event-level detail and raw timing data.
  • Per-thread and per-event information for deep forensic analysis.
  • Required when aggregated rows mask parameter differences.
Decision flow
If you need a fast answer, run sys views. If sys aggregates hide per-event anomalies or you need precise timestamps, query Performance Schema tables like events_statements_history for the event-level trace.
-- Example 1. Run sys.statements_with_runtimes_in_host 2. If a top row looks problematic, run EXPLAIN 3. If behavior varies by parameters, query events_statements_history for per-event detail
Key Takeaway

Use sys for speed and Performance Schema for depth. Combine both for efficient, thorough investigation.

screens.title: Activity: analyze server activity with sys schema
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity guides you through a short sequence to see sys outputs in your environment. First, confirm that Performance Schema is enabled and configured to collect statement and wait events, because sys depends on that instrumentation. Next, run a mixed workload: a few SELECTs, some small UPDATEs, and a SELECT SLEEP(3) to simulate a long-running query. Then run three diagnostic queries: one against sys. processlist to spot active threads, one against statements_with_runtimes_in_host to locate slow statements, and one against io_global_by_file_by_latency to find input and output hot files. For each result, write down one observation and one follow-up action. For example, if processlist shows a connection in a metadata lock state with a high time, your follow-up might be to identify the blocking DDL and coordinate a short maintenance window. If statements_with_runtimes_in_host shows a frequently-executed query with high avg_latency, note plan inspection and EXPLAIN as the next step. If io_global_by_file_by_latency shows a data file with high latency, coordinate with storage to inspect queue depth. This structured lab helps you move from observation to a concrete troubleshooting action list. Activity: analyze server activity with sys schema means practice producing observations and one clear follow-up action for processlist, statement runtimes, and file i/o outputs.. In practical terms, follow a short terminal-style lab to observe results. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › Activity: analyze server activity
Step 1 — Enable instruments
Ensure Performance Schema collects statements and waits. Without instruments, sys views will be incomplete.
Step 2 — Simulate workload
-- Run a mix of statements SELECT 1; SELECT SLEEP(3); UPDATE inventory SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE id = 10;
Step 3 — Run checks and record observations
Run these queries and note one observation and one follow-up action for each.
-- Processlist SELECT thd_id, conn_id, user, db, command, state, time, current_statement FROM sys.processlist WHERE command != 'Sleep' ORDER BY time DESC; -- Slow statements SELECT query, db, exec_count, avg_latency FROM sys.statements_with_runtimes_in_host ORDER BY avg_latency DESC LIMIT 5; -- I/O by file SELECT file, total_read_bytes/1024/1024 AS read_mb, total_written_bytes/1024/1024 AS written_mb, total_latency/1000000000 AS total_latency_ms FROM sys.io_global_by_file_by_latency ORDER BY total_latency DESC LIMIT 5;
Observation template
Observation: Describe what the view shows. Action: One short next step you will take to investigate or mitigate.
Example

Observation: processlist shows a thread waiting on metadata lock for 12s. Action: identify blocking DDL and schedule a quick exclusive operation or kill if safe.

Learning goal

By practicing this sequence you will build a quick triage pattern to convert raw sys outputs into concrete actions.

screens.title: Common mistakes and troubleshooting tips
screens.narratorSegment: Working with sys is efficient, but there are recurring mistakes to avoid. First, forgetting that sys depends on Performance Schema instrumentation is the most common error. If instruments for statements, waits, or file input and output are disabled or filtered, sys views will return empty or misleading results. Always verify instrumentation before trusting summaries. Second, assuming sys always provides the granularity you need can stall investigations. If aggregated rows hide important parameter differences, step into Performance Schema raw tables. Third, changing sys variables without capacity planning can increase memory usage; for example increasing statement history retains more data and may raise resource consumption. Fourth, interpreting time or latency values without context may lead to wrong actions — a high waiting time could be a lock wait, not C P U consumption. For troubleshooting, follow a small checklist: confirm instruments, run sys views to triage, cross-check with EXPLAIN or Performance Schema if results remain unclear, and document configuration changes. A final tip is to always test configuration and queries in staging before production. These habits keep your diagnostics reliable and reproducible.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › Common mistakes
Mistake 1 — Missing instruments

If Performance Schema instruments are disabled, sys views will return empty or partial results. Always verify instrumentation before relying on sys output.

Mistake 2 — Misreading latency

High time may indicate waits, not CPU. Correlate state and other metrics before taking action like killing threads.

Mistake 3 — Over-tuning history

Increasing history size can help post-mortem but may increase memory usage. Test and monitor before applying widely.

Mistake 4 — Stopping at sys

If sys aggregates hide important detail, drill into Performance Schema raw tables for per-event information.

Quick troubleshooting checklist
  1. Confirm Performance Schema instruments are enabled.
  2. Run relevant sys views for a quick triage.
  3. Correlate results with EXPLAIN and raw Performance Schema when needed.
  4. Document and test any sys variable changes in staging.

fullNarratorScript:
The sys schema is an essential convenience layer built on top of Performance Schema that makes raw instrumentation useful without heavy S Q L. In this lesson you will learn why sys exists, what it does for DBAs, and the practical views you will reach for during day-to-day troubleshooting. Think of sys as a translator: it aggregates events, formats latency and memory metrics, and exposes user-friendly views so you can focus on analysis rather than joins. For example, instead of writing several joins across events_statements_history and threads, you can query sys. statements_with_runtimes_in_host to surface the statements ranked by average latency. That reduces both time and error when hunting slow queries or tracking input and output hot spots. We will also cover how to check active sessions with sys. processlist, how to read file-level input and output with io_global_by_file_by_latency, and how to interpret memory allocations via memory_global_by_current_bytes. Finally, you will learn common pitfalls: sys does not collect extra data and depends entirely on Performance Schema instrumentation, and sometimes you must dive into the raw tables for the deepest analysis. By the end of the lesson you will know when sys is sufficient and when to step down into raw Performance Schema data.

Over these screens you will develop practical skills for monitoring and troubleshooting with the sys schema. First, you will be able to explain the purpose and benefits of sys and how it relies on Performance Schema instrumentation. You will practice identifying the most useful sys views for monitoring active sessions, input and output, and memory. You will also learn how to find slow statements quickly using runtime views and full-table-scan reports. Finally, you will see which configurable sys variables affect reporting and history size and how to change them safely. Each objective ties directly to routine DBA tasks: checking active client activity during outage, finding queries for index tuning, pinpointing a noisy file causing input and output latency, and adjusting instrumentation history to retain useful details. Along the way you'll learn to spot a common misconception: sys does not capture additional events—it only presents what Performance Schema already gathers. Understanding that boundary helps you decide when sys alone is enough and when to inspect raw Performance Schema tables for deeper troubleshooting.

This second objectives screen focuses on hands-on capabilities you will practice with sys views. You will learn to inspect memory allocations and interpret current and high-water marks using memory_global_by_current_bytes. You will apply input and output summaries to find which files show the highest latency and read/write bytes using io_global_by_file_by_latency. You will become confident querying statements_with_full_table_scans and statements_with_errors_or_warnings to reduce costly full scans and track problematic statements. You will also learn how to change sys variables that control history or background thread accounting, like ps_setup_size_statements_history, and why those settings matter for what sys displays. Finally, you will be able to list common mistakes and decide when sys is insufficient and raw Performance Schema tables are required for deeper analysis. Each objective includes a short mnemonic and a verified milestone so you can check that you can run the queries, interpret results, and make a short tuning recommendation based on the output.

The sys schema is a curated set of views, functions, and procedures that present Performance Schema data in an aggregated, readable format. In short, it does not collect new events; it reshapes and summarizes the data Performance Schema already captures. A useful analogy is to think of Performance Schema as an instrumented raw log and sys as a set of report templates that turn that log into charts and tables you can read quickly. This means sys saves you time when you need high-level answers — like which queries are slow or which files have the most input and output latency — because the heavy lifting of joins and unit conversions is already done for you. For example, instead of computing average latencies from multiple events tables, you can query statements_with_runtimes_in_host and see avg_latency and max_latency ready to act on. A common misconception is that sys reduces the need to learn Performance Schema; it does not. If you need the lowest-level detail — for instance the exact events or raw wait instances — you must query the Performance Schema tables directly. The practical takeaway is to use sys for routine diagnosis and only step down into raw tables when a deeper, granular trace is required. Try to internalize that boundary now: sys simplifies analysis, Performance Schema provides depth.

When you need to quickly see what the server is doing, sys. processlist is a more usable view than SHOW PROCESSLIST because it provides richer columns and is easier to filter. The typical workflow is to run a SELECT that omits sleeping connections, sort by running time, and inspect the current_statement, state, and time columns. For example, a common triage query selects thd_id, conn_id, user, db, command, state, time, and current_statement and orders by time descending to reveal long-running work. Use this output to spot blocked or stuck queries and note the program or user responsible. A concrete example: after executing a few simple selects and a deliberate sleep, run the provided query and observe a row where command is not Sleep and time is several seconds — that identifies the simulated long-running query. A misconception to watch is assuming high time always means heavy resource use; sometimes a thread waits for a lock with low C P U but high wait time. The key skill is correlating state, current_statement, and time to determine whether to kill, tune, or investigate further. Practice by running the example and describing the state and likely next action for any long entry you find.

To prioritize tuning, start by ranking statements by average latency. The sys. statements_with_runtimes_in_host view exposes avg_latency, total_latency, exec_count, and max_latency so you can see both typical and worst-case behavior. A practical query selects query, db, full_scan, exec_count, total_latency, avg_latency, and max_latency and orders by avg_latency descending. When you run that, look for statements with both high avg_latency and significant exec_count; those are excellent optimization candidates because they compound cost. A concrete scenario: if a reporting query runs often during peak traffic and shows high avg_latency, consider adding indexes, rewriting joins, or breaking the report into smaller queries. A common misconception is to optimize queries with a single high max_latency but zero exec_count; always consider frequency. Also check the full_scan flag — statements that frequently perform full table scans are top candidates for index intervention. Finally, remember that sys aggregates by text; when many similar parameterized statements appear as one row, consider looking at the raw Performance Schema for per-thread detail. The core skill is ranking by avg_latency, correlating with exec_count and full_scan, and creating an actionable list for tuning. Finding slow statements with runtime views means rank by avg_latency and factor in exec_count and full_scan to prioritize which queries to tune first.. In practical terms, use statements_with_runtimes_in_host to rank expensive queries. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Some sys views focus on specific problems. For example, sys. statements_with_full_table_scans collects statements that performed full table scans, exposing full_scan_count, exec_count, and latencies. Another useful view is sys. statements_with_errors_or_warnings, which surfaces statements that caused errors or warnings. The comparison approach is to use the focused view when you have a hypothesis. If slow reports point to scanning behavior, query the full_table_scans view and order by full_scan_count to find the most frequent offenders. If an application reports errors, check the errors_or_warnings view to find statements that generate those events and correlate with user reports. A concrete example: ordering by full_scan_count descending will show a frequently scanned query that might benefit from an index. A misconception is to treat these focused views as exhaustive—they summarize events that Performance Schema recorded, so missing instrumentation or disabled instruments will hide problems. When you need row-level or event-level detail, drill into the underlying Performance Schema tables. Disk activity often explains slow queries more than S Q L structure alone. The sys. io_global_by_file_by_latency view aggregates input and output per file and provides total_read_bytes, total_written_bytes, and total_latency so you can see which files cause the most latency. A typical analysis selects file, total_read_bytes divided to megabytes, total_written_bytes to megabytes, and total_latency converted to milliseconds, ordering by total_latency descending to highlight the most latency-prone files. For instance, InnoDB data files or binary logs may show as top latency contributors. Once you identify a hot file, correlate it with MySQL configuration, file placement, or underlying storage health. It could indicate a need to move data files to faster storage, tune checkpointing settings, or investigate OS-level contention. A common mistake is to interpret high bytes transferred as the same as high latency; high throughput is normal for busy databases, but high total_latency points to delays. Use both bytes and latency together: high latency with modest bytes often means seeks or IO wait; high bytes with low latency suggests healthy throughput. The practical outcome is a prioritized list of files to investigate with storage and input and output tuning actions.

Memory pressure can cause instability and degraded performance. The sys. memory_global_by_current_bytes view reports current_alloc_bytes and high_alloc_bytes so you can see current allocations and recorded high-water marks across components. A useful query selects event_name, current_alloc_bytes / 1024 / 1024 as current_alloc_mb, and high_alloc_bytes / 1024 / 1024 as high_alloc_mb, ordered by current_alloc_bytes descending to surface the biggest consumers. For example, internal buffers or caches may appear as top consumers and point to configuration areas to tune. When you see a component with a large difference between high_alloc and current_alloc, it suggests bursts of activity or temporary spikes; an always-high current_alloc indicates sustained consumption that might require configuration changes. A common misconception is assuming memory reported here directly equals OS process resident memory. These are allocations tracked by Performance Schema for internal components and threads; you still must correlate with OS-level tools for total process memory. The practical path is: identify large allocators in sys, review MySQL configuration or workload causing them, then test changes on a staging instance before production. This view helps make informed memory tuning decisions and avoid out-of-memory surprises.

sys exposes a few variables you can set to control how its views behave, such as ps_setup_size_statements_history which controls how much statement history to keep, and ps_thread_account_for_background_threads which affects whether background threads are included in some aggregations. Use SET GLOBAL sys. variable_name = value to change these settings. The safe process is: first understand your workload and why you need more or less history, then change the variable in a non-production environment and observe effects on view contents and Performance Schema overhead. A concrete example: increasing ps_setup_size_statements_history retains more statements for sys views, which can help with post-facto investigation but increases memory and storage used by Performance Schema. A common pitfall is adjusting these variables without checking Performance Schema instrumentation — if the underlying instruments are not enabled, increasing history does not create data. Another pitfall is to raise history size on a very busy system without capacity planning, which can increase memory pressure. The practical guidance is to document any change, monitor memory and query instrumentation impact, and roll back if Performance Schema metrics show undue overhead. Use sys settings to make views more informative, but always balance visibility with resource cost.

Deciding between using sys and directly querying Performance Schema depends on the level of detail you need. Use sys when you want aggregated, human-friendly summaries for common tasks like ranking slow queries, seeing active sessions, or locating input and output and memory hotspots. The benefit is speed: queries are shorter and results are already formatted. However, sys does not replace Performance Schema for event-level analysis. When you need exact event timing, per-thread stack traces, or low-level wait instances, raw Performance Schema tables such as events_statements_history or events_waits_history provide the granularity sys abstracts away. A practical example: if sys shows a statement with high avg_latency but multiple parameterized variants are aggregated together, stepping down to events_statements_history will show per-thread or per-event details and reveal which parameter values trigger poor performance. A common misconception is that sys is always sufficient for any performance problem; it is not. The pattern to adopt is: start with sys for quick triage, then drill into Performance Schema when sys answers are insufficient. This two-level approach balances speed with depth and prevents wasted time writing complex joins for routine checks.

Working with sys is efficient, but there are recurring mistakes to avoid. First, forgetting that sys depends on Performance Schema instrumentation is the most common error. If instruments for statements, waits, or file input and output are disabled or filtered, sys views will return empty or misleading results. Always verify instrumentation before trusting summaries. Second, assuming sys always provides the granularity you need can stall investigations. If aggregated rows hide important parameter differences, step into Performance Schema raw tables. Third, changing sys variables without capacity planning can increase memory usage; for example increasing statement history retains more data and may raise resource consumption. Fourth, interpreting time or latency values without context may lead to wrong actions — a high waiting time could be a lock wait, not C P U consumption. For troubleshooting, follow a small checklist: confirm instruments, run sys views to triage, cross-check with EXPLAIN or Performance Schema if results remain unclear, and document configuration changes. A final tip is to always test configuration and queries in staging before production. These habits keep your diagnostics reliable and reproducible.
